timelineEvents.title: Multiple-language versions and transnational sound-film production
timelineEvents.label: Transnational sound film
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Before 1933, Kaper and Jurmann were already working within the multiple-language version system that linked Babelsberg, Joinville, Vienna, and other European production centres.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The practice of producing parallel language versions was one of the key industrial conditions of early sound cinema. It allowed music to move more easily than dialogue across national markets, even when lyrics, singers, and performance contexts changed. Kaper and Jurmann’s work in this system gave their songs and professional skills a transnational character before their forced departure from Germany.

places.authorizedName: Studios Paramount, rue des Réservoirs, Saint-Maurice
places.publicNote: Paramount’s French studio stood on the rue des Réservoirs in Saint-Maurice. The trade called it Joinville, after the neighbouring commune, where the Pathé-Natan studios stood on the boulevard Gallieni; Ciné-Miroir set out the difference in 1934. By May 1930 it had five stages under Robert T. Kane and served Paramount’s plan to make talking pictures in six languages; by 1933 it also housed independent productions. In September 1933 Variety placed Erich Pommer’s Fox-Europa unit there as it prepared its next film, which became On a volé un homme, with music by Jurmann and Kaper; in January 1934 it expected the unit to return to “the Paramount Joinville studio”. The marker stands on the rue des Réservoirs and does not outline the studio grounds.
